862.title: The bodhi tree cutting
862.hook: Ashoka's daughter Sanghamitta brings a cutting of the bodhi tree to Anuradhapura, where it still grows
862.howItsDone: Pilgrims visit the bodhi tree at Anuradhapura to offer flowers and water and to sit in meditation, and Sri Lankan Buddhists remember Sanghamitta's arrival at a full moon festival each year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mahinda to Sri Lanka: a monk on a rock, a king with a bow, and a riddle about a mango tree. Your line was the teaching crossed the sea. Who brought it to you? Day eight hundred sixty-two.

On the island, a group of women have a request. Anula, a woman of the royal house, and the women around her have heard Mahinda teach, and they want to leave home and be ordained as nuns. Mahinda says he can't do it: the chronicle has him say it isn't allowed for monks to ordain women. That takes nuns. And there are no nuns on the island. But Mahinda has a sister. So a message goes back across the sea to the emperor, asking for two things: his daughter, and a branch of a tree.
screen: `THE WOMEN ASK TO BE ORDAINED.` → `NO NUNS ON THE ISLAND.` → `SEND FOR A SISTER.`

segments.voice: First, the sister. Sanghamitta is a nun, Ashoka's daughter, and in the Mahavamsa she agrees to go. She'll be the one who can give the island's women what they asked for. Second, the branch. The tree is the bodhi tree, the tree under which the Buddha sat on the night he awoke. The chronicle tells of a branch from it, taken with great ceremony and set in a golden vessel, carried down to the coast and onto a ship, with Sanghamitta beside it. It's one of the chronicle's great set pieces: music, offerings, the sea itself, it says, made calm. Third, the arrival. When the ship comes in, the chronicle says, King Devanampiya Tissa wades into the water up to his neck to receive the branch. There's the image: a king, soaked, holding a pot with a tree in it over his head. The branch is carried to the royal capital, Anuradhapura, and planted in a park there. And Anula and the women around her are ordained by Sanghamitta. The tree and the nuns arrive together. Fourth, it still grows. At Anuradhapura today, a bodhi tree stands behind railings, held up by props, surrounded by flags and pilgrims. Tradition holds that it is that same tree, grown from the branch Sanghamitta brought. Pilgrims come to sit near it, to offer flowers, and to pour water at its roots. Historians may ask what can be proven. The people who sit beneath it are honoring something simpler: a living thing that has been cared for, by many hands, for a very long time.
screen: `A SISTER WHO CAN ORDAIN.` · `A BRANCH IN A GOLDEN VESSEL.` · `THE KING WADES INTO THE SEA.` · `IT STILL GROWS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: care for one plant. If there's a plant near you, go to it, or bring one to mind: a houseplant, a tree on your street, weeds pushing through a sidewalk. Give it a little water if it needs it, or just look at it closely. The color of the leaves. Where it's growing toward the light. Then settle and breathe, and let it be your company for the sit. Something alive, slowly growing, while you sit still. The bell holds the time.
The bodhi tree cutting. A branch of the tree of awakening, carried by Sanghamitta across the sea to Anuradhapura. Today's word.
Your line: it still grows. Today, water something living, or tend to something someone handed down to you, so it keeps growing. Day eight hundred sixty-two.

863.title: Written down
863.hook: in the first century BCE the Pali canon was written on palm leaves at Aluvihara
863.howItsDone: Theravada monasteries keep both ways alive: monks memorize and chant the texts together, and the written canon, once kept on palm leaves, is now printed and studied as well.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bodhi tree cutting: a branch in a golden vessel, a king wading into the sea. Your line was it still grows. Did you water something living? Day eight hundred sixty-three.

A strip of dried palm leaf, long and narrow, lies across a monk's knee. He holds a metal stylus and scratches letters into its surface, line after careful line. Later, soot and oil will be rubbed across the leaf and wiped away, and the dark will stay only in the scratches, so the words appear. A whole library can be made this way, one leaf at a time, tied between wooden boards. In Sri Lanka, the chronicle says, there came a day when the monks decided the teaching had to be written down in books.
screen: `A STRIP OF PALM LEAF.` → `A STYLUS SCRATCHES LETTERS.` → `THE MONKS DECIDE.`

segments.voice: First, a teaching that lived in voices. Earlier in these weeks we heard how the teaching was carried by memory: monks learned the discourses and the rules by heart, and chanted them together, so a mistake by one could be caught by the others. The chronicles of Sri Lanka say that the three baskets of the teaching, and the commentaries on them, had been handed down that way, by mouth. Second, the fear. The Mahavamsa sets this moment in the reign of King Vattagamani, a troubled reign, in which the king himself is driven from his throne for a time. The chronicle says the monks saw that people were falling away, and they came together and wrote the texts down in books, so that the true teaching might endure. That's the whole reason it gives. Not convenience. Survival. Third, the place. Tradition names the spot as Aluvihara, a monastery among great rocks, where the work is said to have been done. Pilgrims still visit it. Fourth, what changed and what didn't. Writing didn't end the chanting. Monks still learn texts by heart and recite them together, and in monasteries today the voice is still one way the teaching is received. But from then on there was a second keeper, a quieter one: leaves in a bundle, waiting for anyone who could read. When a manuscript wore out, it could be copied fresh. That's the old way a text stays alive, the way a tree does: not by never changing, but by being renewed. The monks at Aluvihara didn't know who would read their leaves. They wrote for strangers, so the teaching wouldn't depend on any one memory, or any one life.
screen: `A TEACHING THAT LIVED IN VOICES.` · `AFRAID IT COULD BE LOST.` · `WRITTEN AT ALUVIHARA.` · `CHANTING GOES ON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write down one line. Find paper and a pen if you can, or a note on your phone if you can't. Choose one line that matters to you: something from these lessons, a saying from someone you love, a line from a text of your own tradition. Write it slowly, letter by letter, the way the monk scratched each letter into the leaf. Read it back once. Then put the pen down, settle, and let the line rest with you while you breathe. The bell holds the time.
Written down. The moment, as the chronicle tells it, when the teaching carried by voices was set down in books, so it would endure. Today's word.
Your line: on palm leaves. Today, keep the line you wrote somewhere you'll see it again, and read it once more before you sleep. Day eight hundred sixty-three.

864.title: The stupas
864.hook: Sanchi and Bharhut: great mounds holding relics, walked around clockwise
864.howItsDone: At stupas and pagodas, Buddhist pilgrims walk clockwise, sometimes three times, sometimes chanting or carrying flowers and incense, as an act of respect and meditation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, written down: the teaching set on palm leaves so it would endure. Your line was on palm leaves. Did you keep the line you wrote, and read it again? Day eight hundred sixty-four.

A dome of brick and stone, rounded like an upturned bowl, rises out of a hilltop in central India. Around it runs a stone railing, and through the railing, carved gateways, crowded with elephants, trees, people, whole stories in relief. Pilgrims don't go inside. There is no inside to go to. They walk around it, slowly, always in the same direction. This is the great stupa at Sanchi. Today's word is the shape itself.
screen: `A DOME LIKE AN UPTURNED BOWL.` → `CARVED GATEWAYS.` → `NO INSIDE. THEY WALK AROUND.`

segments.voice: First, the Buddha's own instruction. In the Great Discourse on the final passing, Ananda asks what should be done with the Teacher's body. The Buddha answers that it should be treated like the remains of a great king, and a stupa built at a place where four roads meet. Whoever brings a garland or scent there, or bows, or simply grows calm in heart there, he says, it will be for their good and their happiness for a long time. Second, the relics shared. After the cremation, the same discourse tells, the peoples who had loved him each asked for a share of the remains, and each built a stupa over theirs. So from the start, the stupa is a mound with something precious at its heart, sealed in, out of sight. Third, Sanchi and Bharhut. These are stupas in India whose stone railings and gateways survive, and they're covered with carvings: the Jataka tales we met earlier, scenes from the Buddha's life, spirits of the trees, ordinary people bringing offerings. Some of the carvings carry the names of the people who paid for them. Monks, nuns, merchants, villagers, their small gifts carved into the stone. Fourth, walking around it. Pilgrims circle a stupa keeping it on their right, which means walking clockwise. It's an old Indian gesture of respect. In the suttas, people who visit the Buddha often leave the same way, keeping him on their right as they go. At a stupa, the whole visit is that gesture, done again and again. The body moves. The center stays still. And the walk itself becomes the prayer, or the meditation, or simply a way of saying: this matters, and I came.
screen: `A MOUND WHERE FOUR ROADS MEET.` · `THE RELICS SHARED OUT.` · `GATEWAYS FULL OF STORIES.` · `KEEP IT ON YOUR RIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk once around something, clockwise. Choose something near you: a table, a chair, a plant, a tree outside. Stand facing it, then walk slowly around it, keeping it on your right. Feel each foot land. Let it be slow enough that it feels deliberate. When you're back where you began, pause, and if it feels right, bow your head a little. Then sit, and breathe, and let the circle settle. If walking isn't possible today, trace the circle with your eyes or your hand. The bell holds the time.
Stupa. A mound holding relics, at the center of a path that pilgrims walk around, keeping it on their right. Today's word.
Your line: walk around it. Today, when you're stuck on something, walk once around the block or the room before you decide, and let the circle slow you down. Day eight hundred sixty-four.

865.title: The empty throne
865.hook: early art showed the Buddha by symbols only: a footprint, a wheel, a tree, an empty seat
865.howItsDone: Buddhists still honor the Buddha through symbols like the wheel of dhamma, carved footprints and the bodhi tree, alongside statues, and pilgrims bow and leave offerings before them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the stupa: a mound with relics at its heart, and pilgrims circling it. Your line was walk around it. Did you walk a slow circle before deciding something? Today, back to those carved gateways, for a closer look. Day eight hundred sixty-five.

On a carved stone panel, a crowd has gathered. People kneel with their hands together. Some hold flowers. Above them spreads a great tree, every leaf cut into the stone, and beneath the tree is a seat. A throne, with a cushion on it. Everyone is facing it, bowing to it. And the seat is empty. Nobody is sitting there. On panel after panel of the old railings and gateways, the scene repeats. The Buddha's life is everywhere in the stone, and the Buddha, it seems, is nowhere.
screen: `A CROWD KNEELS.` → `A TREE, A SEAT.` → `THE SEAT IS EMPTY.`

segments.voice: First, the signs. In the carvings at places like Bharhut and Sanchi, the Buddha's great moments are shown, but he isn't, at least not as a human figure. The awakening is a tree with an empty seat beneath it. The first teaching is a wheel, the wheel of dhamma set turning. His presence is a pair of footprints, or a parasol held over no one. A riderless horse leaves the palace. The stories are all there, and the center of each story is a space. Second, a teaching about the one who has gone out. The suttas don't describe these carvings. But one passage sits beside them well. In the Sutta Nipata, a seeker named Upasiva asks the Buddha what becomes of one who has reached the end. The Buddha answers with a flame. A flame blown out by the wind comes to rest and can't be counted any more. So with the sage: there is no measure for him, nothing left by which to say he is this or that. Some readers see the empty seat as that teaching in stone. Third, the other reading. Some scholars read these carvings differently. They suggest that some of the scenes show later pilgrims worshiping at the holy places, the tree, the seat, the footprints, rather than the Buddha's own moments with him left out. Both readings are held by serious people, and the stone itself doesn't settle it. Fourth, what the absence does. Whichever reading is right, a visitor to these panels can't stare at a face. You have to look at what he left: a teaching, a path, a place where someone sat down and woke up. The seat is left open.
screen: `A TREE, A WHEEL, A FOOTPRINT.` · `NO MEASURE FOR ONE GONE OUT.` · `SCHOLARS READ IT TWO WAYS.` · `THE SPACE INVITES YOU IN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: draw a simple symbol. With a pen on paper, or a finger on your palm, or on the table in front of you, draw one of them slowly. A circle with spokes, for the wheel. The outline of a footprint. A small square seat with nothing on it. Don't make it good. Make it slow. Then look at what you drew, and at the empty part of it, the space inside the lines. Settle, and breathe, and let that space be enough. The bell holds the time.
The empty throne. A seat beneath the tree with no one on it, the way old carvings showed the Buddha by what he left. Today's word.
Your line: shown by absence. Today, notice one empty chair, one quiet space, one gap someone has left, and let it remind you of what they gave. Day eight hundred sixty-five.

866.title: The first images
866.hook: in Gandhara and Mathura, the first statues of the Buddha appear
866.howItsDone: Buddhists today bow before images of the Buddha and offer flowers, candles and incense, and the wheel and footprint remain in use beside them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the empty throne: a tree, a wheel, a seat with no one on it. Your line was shown by absence. What empty space did you notice? Today, someone sits down on that seat. Day eight hundred sixty-six.

Two statues stand in a museum, a few steps apart. Both are the Buddha. The first is carved in gray stone: wavy hair, a calm face, a heavy robe falling in deep folds over both shoulders, a body that looks as if it could breathe. The second is carved in reddish stone: a rounder face, broad shoulders, one shoulder bare, a slight smile, a hand raised with the palm out. They come from two different regions, Gandhara and Mathura. After the empty seat, the Buddha has a face. In fact, he has two.
screen: `TWO STATUES.` → `GRAY STONE, RED STONE.` → `THE BUDDHA HAS A FACE.`

segments.voice: First, Gandhara. In the northwest, where trade roads crossed and many peoples met, carvers made Buddhas with flowing hair and robes in deep, rippling folds. Art historians see in them the touch of Greek and Roman sculpture, which had reached that region. The Buddha stands like a figure from a classical temple, but his eyes are lowered, and he is still. Second, Mathura. Further south and east, in the city of Mathura, carvers worked in a reddish sandstone. Their Buddhas are fuller, broad-chested, often smiling, with a thin robe that clings to the body. They look strong and present, ready to speak. Third, the question nobody can settle. Which came first? Scholars have argued about it for a long time, and they still disagree. Some look to Gandhara, some to Mathura, and some think the two began around the same time, each in its own way. It's honest to leave it open. Fourth, the signs that stayed. Whatever the style, the new images carried marks that meant something. A rise on the crown of the head. A small mark between the eyebrows. Long earlobes, stretched, tradition says, by the heavy earrings of the prince he once was. And the hands: one raised, palm out, in the gesture often read as do not fear. The empty seat had said, he is gone beyond measure. The statue says something else: he was here, and this is what a calm human being can look like. Buddhist art goes on holding both. The images didn't replace the wheel and the footprint. They sat down beside them.
screen: `GANDHARA: WAVY HAIR, DEEP FOLDS.` · `MATHURA: RED STONE, A SMILE.` · `WHICH CAME FIRST? STILL DEBATED.` · `THE HAND THAT SAYS DO NOT FEAR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at an early Buddha image. If you can, find a picture of a Gandhara or a Mathura Buddha on your phone, or bring to mind any image of the Buddha you've seen. Look slowly. Start at the hands. Then the shoulders. Then the face: the eyes, the mouth. Notice what the carver chose to show. Then close your eyes and sit, and see if any of that stillness can settle into your own face and hands. The bell holds the time.
The first images. Statues of the Buddha from Gandhara and Mathura, after the old art had shown him only by signs. Today's word.
Your line: a face appears. Today, look at one face, someone you love or a stranger in a photo, the way you looked at the statue: slowly, without judging. Day eight hundred sixty-six.

867.title: The Greek king's questions
867.hook: King Menander, a Greek ruler in India, questions the monk Nagasena (Milinda, Book 2)
867.howItsDone: Theravada monks and students read the Questions of King Milinda as a guide to hard questions, and teachers still retell its similes, like the chariot, when explaining the teaching on self.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first images. After footprints, wheels and an empty seat, a face appears in stone. Your line was a face appears. Did any face stay with you? Today, a voice: a king who wants answers. Day eight hundred sixty-seven.

A king rides out of his city with a crowd of courtiers, restless for a debate. The book that tells his story describes him as clever and fond of argument, a man who has questioned teacher after teacher and left each one tongue-tied. Nobody, his courtiers admit, can stand up to him anymore. Then someone mentions a monk who has just arrived, a monk named Nagasena. The king goes to see him. The king's name is Milinda in the Pali book, and historians link him with Menander, a Greek ruler in the northwest of India. The book is called the Questions of King Milinda. Today, before a single answer, we look at how the questions are asked.
screen: `A KING WHO WINS EVERY ARGUMENT.` → `A MONK NAMED NAGASENA.` → `THE QUESTIONS OF KING MILINDA.`

segments.voice: First, the setting. The book opens in Sagala, a rich city the text describes with its parks, gates and markets, and it places the city in the country of the Yonakas, the Greeks. So the conversation it records is a meeting of two worlds: a Greek king and a Buddhist monk, talking in India. Second, the ground rules. Early in their talks the king asks whether Nagasena will keep discussing with him. Nagasena says yes, if the king talks as a scholar talks, and no, if he talks as a king talks. The king asks what the difference is. When scholars talk, Nagasena explains, they explain and are explained to, they correct and are corrected, and they don't get angry about it. When kings talk, they state a view, and whoever disagrees is punished. The king agrees to talk as a scholar. Third, the questions themselves. They are not polite. Who is it that keeps the precepts, if there is no self? Is the one who is reborn the same person or someone else? If the Buddha was free of every bad deed, why did he ever feel pain? The king asks what a skeptic would ask, and the book lets him ask it at full strength. Fourth, why this matters. The Theravada tradition kept this book and still teaches from it. So a text Buddhists value is built out of an outsider's hardest questions, asked in good faith and answered patiently, with the king's doubts left in plain view. Over the next days we will hear Nagasena's answers, one at a time: a chariot, a flame, a stolen mango, a pot of milk.
screen: `SAGALA: A GREEK KING IN INDIA.` · `TALK AS A SCHOLAR, NOT AS A KING.` · `HARD QUESTIONS, ASKED AT FULL STRENGTH.` · `A TREASURED BOOK OF AN OUTSIDER'S QUESTIONS.` · then, large: `CORRECT AND BE CORRECTED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one sincere question. Settle and let the breath slow. Think of something you actually don't understand, about this path, about someone in your life, about yourself. Not a trap, not a question you already know the answer to. A real one. Say it to yourself plainly, the way the king might. Then notice how it feels to hold a question without rushing to win it. Leave it open, and rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Milinda. The king of the Questions of King Milinda, linked by historians with the Greek ruler Menander, who asks the monk Nagasena everything. Today's word.
Your line: the king's questions. Today, ask one person one honest question, and talk as a scholar does: ready to be corrected, without getting angry. Day eight hundred sixty-seven.

868.title: The chariot
868.hook: is the chariot the axle, the wheels, the pole? "Nagasena" is a name for parts together (Milinda, Book 2)
868.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use the chariot simile from the Questions of King Milinda, together with the nun Vajira's verse, to explain not-self: a name is used for parts working together, with no fixed core behind them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the king's questions: Milinda meets Nagasena, and they agree to talk as scholars. This week the teaching took root. A bodhi tree cutting that still grows, a canon on palm leaves, stupas to walk around, an empty throne, a first face in stone, and a king with questions. Today, his first one. Day eight hundred sixty-eight.

The king asks the simplest question there is: what's your name? And the monk gives an answer nobody at court expects. He's called Nagasena, he says. That's what his parents and his fellow monks call him. But it's only a name, a way of speaking. No lasting person is found behind it. The king turns to his courtiers, half amused, half offended. If there's no person here, he says, then who wears these robes? Who keeps the rules? Who gets the credit when someone gives alms, and who's to blame if someone harms you? Nagasena doesn't argue. He asks the king how he got here today.
screen: `WHAT'S YOUR NAME?` → `ONLY A NAME, A WAY OF SPEAKING.` → `THEN WHO WEARS THE ROBES?`

segments.voice: First, the chariot at the door. The king came by chariot, he says, not on foot. So Nagasena asks him to point to it. Is the pole the chariot? No. The axle? No. The wheels? No. The frame, the yoke, the reins? No, no, no. Then is the chariot all of these together? No. Something apart from them? No again. Second, the turn. Nagasena springs his own words back on him: then there is no chariot, and the king has told a falsehood in front of his whole court. The courtiers cheer for the monk. And the king, to his credit, works it out aloud. He hasn't lied, he says. Chariot is the name used for the pole, the axle, the wheels, the frame and the rest, when they come together. Third, the point. Just so, Nagasena says. Nagasena is the name used for this body, these feelings, perceptions, mental formations and consciousness, when they come together. Nothing is hidden behind the parts; the name is real as a name. Then Nagasena recalls a verse spoken by a nun named Vajira in the older suttas: where the parts are gathered, people say chariot; where the parts of a life are present, people say a being. The king praises the answer. Fourth, what this does and doesn't say. It doesn't say Nagasena isn't there, or that names are lies. The king still rides home in his chariot. It says a name points to parts working together, not to a fixed core inside them. Buddhists call this anatta, not-self, and this simile is one of the ways teachers still explain it. A chariot gets you across town just fine. It just can't be found apart from its parts.
screen: `IS THE POLE THE CHARIOT? THE WHEELS?` · `THE KING WORKS IT OUT ALOUD.` · `NAGASENA: A NAME FOR PARTS TOGETHER.` · `THE CHARIOT STILL CARRIES HIM HOME.` · then, large: `A NAME FOR PARTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take one thing apart in your mind. Pick something near you: a cup, a chair, a phone. Name its parts, slowly. The handle. The rim. The base. Where, among those parts, is the cup itself? Then, gently, turn the same question toward your own name. A body breathing. Feelings coming and going. Thoughts. Notice what the name points to. No need to reach a conclusion. Just watch the parts working together, and rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
The chariot. Nagasena's simile: neither the pole nor the wheels nor anything apart from them is the chariot, and chariot is a name for the parts together. Today's word.
Your line: a name for parts. Today, when you hear your own name, notice the parts it gathers up: a body, a mood, a thought. Day eight hundred sixty-eight.

fork.setup: you're the king. you rode here by chariot, and the monk has made you deny that the pole, the wheels, and every other part is the chariot. what do you say?
options: fine, then there is no chariot.
the chariot is a hidden thing beyond the parts.
chariot is the name used for the parts together.
fork.reveal: the king works it out: he hasn't lied, because chariot is the name used when the parts come together. Nagasena says, just so with his own name.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit: chariot. the simile Nagasena uses for his own name.

trapdoor: what you thought: a riddle that proves nobody exists.
what it means: a name is real as a name, and it points to parts working together, not to a fixed core inside them.
what a scholar hears: Nagasena backs the simile with the nun Vajira's verse from the Samyutta Nikaya; the teaching is anatta, not-self.
